title: The Sons of Israel and the House of Judah
summary: The chapter names Jacob's twelve sons and then turns at once to Judah, tracing his family through Tamar's son Perez to Hezron. From Hezron's three sons it follows the line of Ram down to Jesse and his seventh son, David, and then sets out the large clans of Caleb and Jerahmeel, with their towns in the hill country of Judah.
story: Chapter 1 moved from Adam to Edom, clearing the ground. Now the Chronicler reaches Israel itself, and after a single verse naming the twelve sons of Jacob he goes straight to Judah, the fourth son. Judah comes first because Judah is the tribe of David, and David is where the book is heading. In the middle of this long list, almost quietly, stands the line from Ram to Boaz to Jesse and then to David, born seventh (verse 15). Everything in the chapter is arranged around that name. Judah's family also carries shadows: a firstborn put to death for wickedness, a son born to Tamar in a story of deceit, and Achar, who brought trouble on Israel. The royal line is not presented as spotless. It is presented as chosen.
historical:
Most of the names in this chapter come from earlier books: Genesis 38 and 46 for Judah's sons, Ruth 4 for the line from Perez to David, Joshua 7 for the sin of Achan, and 1 Samuel for David's brothers. The long lists of the clans of Caleb and Jerahmeel (verses 18 to 55) are found nowhere else in the Bible, and the Chronicler must have had other records. These clans lived in the southern hill country and the Negev. In 1 Samuel 27:10 and 30:29 the Jerahmeelites appear as a distinct group in the south, and the Calebites were linked with Hebron, which Joshua gave to Caleb son of Jephunneh (Joshua 14:13-14). How that famous Caleb relates to Caleb son of Hezron in this chapter is not certain; he may be a later member of the same clan. By David's time they had been absorbed into Judah.

Many of the names here are towns: Tekoa, Ziph, Mareshah, Hebron, Beth-zur, Kiriath-jearim, and Bethlehem are said to have a father, meaning a founder or leading family. For readers in the Persian period, several of these places lay inside or near the small province of Judah where they lived, while others, including Hebron, lay to the south in territory then held largely by Edomites. Naming them was a way of remembering what the whole tribe had once been.
cultural:
Ancient Israel reckoned inheritance through sons, and a family without a son was in danger of losing its name and land. The chapter records several ways a line could continue anyway. Judah's line runs through Tamar, his daughter-in-law, whose story in Genesis 38 turns on this very problem. Sheshan had only daughters, so he gave one of them in marriage to his Egyptian servant Jarha, and the family line continued through their son (verses 34 and 35). Hezron married the daughter of Machir, a Manassite from Gilead, and so a Judahite family took root east of the Jordan (verses 21 to 23).

The list also shows how open these families were. Judah's first wife was a Canaanite, Bath-shua. Abigail's son Amasa had an Ishmaelite father (verse 17). A servant from Egypt becomes the ancestor of thirteen generations. The Kenites of verse 55, linked to the house of Rechab, were originally a non-Israelite people attached to Israel since the time of Moses. The genealogy of the royal tribe is anything but a pure bloodline.
literary: After the list of the twelve sons (verses 1 and 2), the chapter works through Judah's descendants using Hezron's three sons, Jerahmeel, Ram, and Caleb (verse 9). The material is arranged so that Ram's line and David come first, then Caleb's family (verses 18 to 24), then Jerahmeel's (verses 25 to 41), and finally more of Caleb's (verses 42 to 55). Some scholars see a concentric pattern here, with the lists framing one another around a center. The lists themselves are dry, but brief notes break in and tell small stories: a firstborn slain by the LORD, a thief who troubled Israel, a son born to a man of sixty, a servant who became a son-in-law. The Chronicler uses those short notes to carry meaning.

outline.t: Judah's sons, Tamar, and the line of Zerah
Hezron's sons and the line from Ram to David
The family of Caleb son of Hezron
More descendants of Caleb and the clans of Judah's towns

doctrines.note: God's choice of David's line runs through ordinary, tangled family history. The fourth son's tribe is listed first, the seventh son becomes king, and the line survives scandal and loss because God is carrying it forward.

Two brief notes name sin plainly: Er was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and Achar was unfaithful and brought trouble upon Israel. The Chronicler does not hide the wrongs in the royal tribe; he records them as warnings.

The chapter shows the covenant family widening to include Canaanites, Ishmaelites, and an Egyptian. Membership in Israel was rooted in God's covenant with Abraham's family, which from the start had room for outsiders who were joined to it.

words.note: Maal, to act unfaithfully or break faith, used of Achar in verse 7 (the BSB renders the idea as violating the ban). It is one of the Chronicler's key words. It describes treachery against God, taking what belongs to him or giving him less than his due, and it will explain the fall of Saul (10:13) and the exile of Judah (9:1).

Akar, to trouble or bring disaster. The Chronicler spells the thief's name Achar, not Achan as in Joshua 7, so that his name sounds like what he did: Achar the troubler. Joshua 7 makes the same wordplay with the Valley of Achor, where Achan was judged.

Herem, a thing devoted to God, often by destruction. In the conquest, certain cities and their goods were placed under this ban, set apart for God alone. Achan's theft of devoted things from Jericho was not simple stealing; it was taking from God what had been given entirely to him.

David, whose name appears here for the first time in the book, as the seventh son of Jesse (verse 15). The whole genealogy of Judah is shaped around him, and the rest of 1 Chronicles will be his story.

christ: The line from Perez through Hezron, Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon, Boaz, Obed, and Jesse to David (verses 5 and 9 to 15) is the same line that Matthew 1:3-6 uses for Jesus' genealogy, and Luke 3:31-33 follows it too. Matthew even names Tamar, one of the few women in his list. This chapter is one of the Old Testament records that shows how the promise to David rested on an actual family line that could be traced. It also shows the kind of family God worked through: a line that included a Canaanite wife, a daughter-in-law's desperate scheme, and outsiders brought in. The New Testament presents Jesus as the son of David from this very tribe, and Hebrews 7:14 notes that our Lord was descended from Judah.

hard.q: Was David the seventh son of Jesse, as here, or the eighth, as 1 Samuel says?
hard.a: First Chronicles 2:13-15 names seven sons of Jesse and calls David the seventh. First Samuel 16:10-11 and 17:12 say Jesse had eight sons, with David the youngest. Interpreters offer a few explanations. One common view is that one of the brothers died young or without descendants and was left out of the genealogy, which records the lines that continued. Some also point out that genealogies in the ancient world were often shaped to use meaningful numbers, and seven was a number of fullness; placing David seventh may emphasize his importance. Others suggest that one of the eight in Samuel may have been a relative counted with the household. The Bible doesn't settle the question, and the two accounts agree on the point that matters to both: David was the youngest son of Jesse, chosen over his older brothers.

questions: The royal line of Judah includes wickedness, scandal, and outsiders. How does that shape your picture of the kind of people God works through?
Achar's name became a byword for bringing trouble on the whole community. How can one person's unfaithfulness affect the people around them?
Several families in this chapter faced the loss of their name and line and found another way forward. Where have you seen God keep a future open that seemed closed?
